title: Lincoln Appoints the Man Who Snubbed Him
text:
In 1855 Abraham Lincoln, then a lawyer in Illinois, was hired for a major patent case, McCormick v. Manny, to be heard in Cincinnati. He prepared carefully. But the defense team also included Edwin Stanton, a prominent attorney from Pittsburgh, who treated the lanky lawyer from the prairie with contempt. Lincoln was pushed aside, his brief was never used, and by later accounts Stanton refused to work with him. Lincoln went home hurt.

Seven years later Lincoln was President and the War Department was in disarray under Simon Cameron. In January 1862 Lincoln chose as the new Secretary of War the same Edwin Stanton, a Democrat who had also been a sharp critic of his administration. Lincoln judged that Stanton's energy, honesty and organizing ability mattered more than the old insult.

Stanton was hard, abrasive and often clashed with the President, but he ran the war effort with great force, and over the years he came to respect and love Lincoln. He was at Lincoln's bedside when he died in April 1865.
lesson: When choosing people for an important job, weigh what they can do, not how they once treated you. Setting aside a personal slight can win you a capable and loyal ally.
location: Cincinnati, Ohio, and Washington, D.C., USA
source: Doris Kearns Goodwin, Team of Rivals (2005); Benjamin P. Thomas and Harold M. Hyman, Stanton (1962)
caveat: Some of the harshest words attributed to Stanton in 1855 come from later recollections and may be embellished.
